content:
When the James Beard Foundation announced its national culinary awards this summer, both the hospitality industry and the general public tuned in to see who topped the list in each category. Big winners included Los Angeles’s Kato for best wine program, Scotch Lodge in Portland, Ore., for outstanding bar, Philadelphia’s Kalaya for outstanding restaurant, and NYC’s Lei, which took home the prize as the country’s best new restaurant.

On one level, that last award was hardly surprising. Not long after it opened in mid-2025, Lei picked up glowing reviews in The New York Times — as an NYT Critic’s Pick — and The New Yorker, as well as positive writeups in places like Eater and TimeOut. In large part, the critics had already spoken. The JBF was simply confirming what a lot of influential diners with notebooks seemed to be thinking.

But if you’re someone who checks the fine print, you might have noticed something slightly unexpected about Lei’s prize. On its website, the country’s “best new restaurant” describes itself as a “wine bar.”

That’s not a completely new trend: Food-focused wine bars have been claiming more and more of the spotlight — and a similar share of the discourse — in recent years. That said, this award appears to mark its high point to date, at least Stateside. Insiders note that the movement of branding restaurants as wine bars is now spreading around the world, thanks to the many advantages it offers in terms of managing customer expectations, to say nothing of benefits to the bottom line.

Signals and Messaging

Jarl de Vries is managing director at two Amsterdam-based food and drink consultancies, Studio Numen and Cocktail Professor, which design and build beverage programs for both luxury hotel groups and private clients across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and the U.S. In his eyes, calling a dining venue a “wine bar” is a growing trend globally. The term reassures customers about multiple aspects of the experience, he says.

“We see this more and more often, especially in the last couple of years, that places that are called wine bars actually do loads of other stuff, like food, bites, events, and whatnot,” he says. “Having good wine is a signal to guests that everything else is good.”

At Lei, the flaky shao bing, crunchy celtuce, and sweet-and-sour short rib might be the talk of the town, but the broad-reaching wine program is its raison d’être. “The wine list comes first; the food options were designed to eat well alongside a wide range of wine,” says a spokesperson for the restaurant.

For Jonathan Pogash, founder and owner of The Cocktail Guru, a bar and restaurant consultancy, the first big benefit to calling a dining venue a “wine bar” is about customer expectations. Above all, it creates the impression that dinner is not going to be overly formal or stuffy.

“What we see in this trend in these types of bars, even though they’re restaurants as well, is a different type of service. It signals a social experience. It’s just more casual and more open.”

“There is this trend towards the casualization of fine dining,” he says. “That is probably due to the economy and coming out of Covid and trying to compete.”

If the trend wasn’t exactly born then, it certainly seems to have picked up steam around that time. In The New York Times, Eric Asimov wrote about “full-fledged restaurants” calling themselves wine bars and what differentiates a wine bar from a restaurant in late 2022.

Of course, wine bars predate Covid by many decades, if not several centuries. What differs from an original bar à vin in the Old World — and the popular variations on that theme that spread across the U.S. in the first two decades of this century — is the heightened emphasis on high-level cooking that goes far beyond charcuterie and cheese boards.

In addition, de Vries notes, the global “restaurant as wine bar” trend has another quirk, often putting much more emphasis on natural, skin-contact, and low-intervention bottles.

“It’s a particular kind of direction of wine bars, rather than ‘wine’ in general,” he says.

Beyond the list, de Vries says that the global “wine bar” trend has a few particular characteristics that include high quality food in smaller portions that are designed around sharing, as well as a special approach at the front of house.

“What we see in this trend in these types of bars, even though they’re restaurants as well, is a different type of service,” he says. “It signals a social experience. It’s just more casual and more open.”

The design and atmosphere is often different, too, with a greater focus on conversation and conviviality. In short, the trend is not just about nomenclature. It’s an entire worldview.

“It basically extends to everything else in the venue,” he says. “Food, service, design, atmosphere. We see this quite often.”

Better Wines, Better Margins

In part, what you call your place is about creating expectations and atmosphere. But it can also be about cash flow.

One of the best new restaurants in the beautiful, canal-lined city of Bruges, Belgium, is Cult, a wine-forward venue which opened in late 2024. On its website, it describes itself as “Wijnbar & Apero, Restaurant,” covering three categories at once.

Co-founder Kees Dobbelaar says that Cult’s multi-part definition was inspired by his team’s earlier experience at Blend, a beloved and still-running local bar that initially had “almost no food,” frequently causing its guests to bail out after a drink or two, until Blend started serving small bites as well.

Although their new venue, Cult, has an extensive kitchen and serves dry-aged steaks, among other big-ticket fare, calling it a “wine bar” makes guests feel like they can come in at any time of day, for any reason.

“There’s no pressure at all,” he says. “If you want to come in for one glass, no problem. You want to have three glasses? Perfect, also fine. You can have three small snacks and one glass. Whatever.”

Ideally, he says, the term “wine bar” will reassure guests that they won’t have to order a three-course menu. “For us, one of the most important things is that it is very accessible.”

In terms of the menu, that accessibility includes tapas-style dishes, as well as small hot plates like garnished oysters and toasted brioche with smoked eel, which is sold as a perfect pairing for a glass of Champagne.

The term also helps keep things busy.

“In a restaurant, a table or a chair is used once for lunch and once for dinner,” he says. “In a wine bar, every seat is taken 10 times for service. That’s a different, more economic part of the job.”

Another economic advantage to branding a restaurant as a wine bar can be lower operating costs, Pogash adds. Putting the emphasis on wine can mean that operators don’t necessarily have to stock spirits, train staff on cocktails, or buy a pricey liquor license.

“There’s no pressure at all. If you want to come in for one glass, no problem. You want to have three glasses? Perfect, also fine. You can have three small snacks and one glass. Whatever.”

It can also change the expectation of how drinks are sold. That, too, can be part of the business plan.

“When I think of a ‘wine bar,’ I think of a glass of wine,” Pogash says. “Just from an operator’s standpoint, it’s probably more efficient to serve glasses — multiple glasses — than have people buy bottles. You’re going to get a better markup on your glasses of wine.”

Obligations to Tradition

Although “wine bar” might be a popular way to brand eating and drinking venues at the moment, many terms have similarly come into fashion and since disappeared. In the Western United States, the popularity of the term “saloon” declined precipitously after about 1900 or so, while Google Books Ngram Viewer shows a peak for “bar and grill” in 1944, a big slide in popularity until roughly 1977, another rise until 2012, followed by another slip. Pogash cites “kitchen and cocktails,” “bar and cocktails,” and “chophouse” as once-trendy names that hardly get used anymore.

Such changes regularly run through most segments of the drinks industry, in almost every country. In recent years, the U.K. has seen an increase in beer-focused venues that eschew the traditional term pub, instead calling themselves taprooms, even when they don’t actually brew their own beer. Daisy Turnell, co-owner and director at Tipple Marketing, cites it as another take on how self-branding can influence customer expectations, while also meaning fewer obligations to longstanding tradition for venue operators.

“I think that ‘taproom’ makes you think of a modern and innovative beer-focused venue,” she says. “It’s a bit more freeing than saying ‘pub,’ which can lead to a variety of expectations in advance.”

Regardless of what owners are choosing to call these venues, Pogash believes they’re mostly using the same winning formula.

“Whether it’s cocktails and food or wine and food, pairing food with drinks is huge,” he says. “That will pretty much never go away.”

content:
We all have them: those breweries we can’t believe aren’t being shouted out from the rooftops. The vibes are immaculate, the service is great, and the beer hits all the right notes. It’s your favorite place to visit, and you’re half-tempted to keep it all to yourself. But you also know that everyone deserves to enjoy this underrated gem.

In the craft beer world, the East Coast is known for heavy hitters. Breweries like The Alchemist, Tree House, Allagash, Trillium, and Other Half have developed cult followings and made beers that defined the industry over the past few decades. But what about the lesser-known places? To uncover the breweries that may not be as famous but deserve more attention, we decided to ask the people who know best: brewers.

They shouted out places with great hospitality, intentional beers, unique drinking experiences, and humble brewers. And one quality stood out. Multiple brewers noted producers that use locally grown ingredients, with one source calling a farm-focused approach “the future of brewing in the States.”

From beloved farm breweries in New England to a lager-focused spot in the Outer Banks, these are the breweries that deserve a bit more notice and applause.

The most underrated East Coast breweries, according to brewers:

  • Norbrook Farm Brewery
  • Fine Creek Brewing
  • Fox Farm Brewery
  • The Brewery at Four Star Farms
  • Hot Plate Brewing
  • Whalehead Brewing
  • Plan Bee Brewery
  • Benchtop Brewing
  • Urban Garden Brewing
  • Hourglass Brewing
  • Anyone exclusively brewing with East Coast ingredients

“Norbrook Farm Brewery in Connecticut. One of the best settings in New England, and the owner is typically on-site with great customer service” —Bob Foley, co-owner, Foley Brothers Brewing, Brandon, Vt.

“Fine Creek Brewing. Located in Powhatan, Va. (just west of Richmond), Fine Creek doesn’t just check all the boxes; it decimates them. Their tagline is ‘Home Grown x Made With Intention,’ and it couldn’t be more true. For me, it all starts with the brew team and Brian Mandeville. There’s no style he can’t make and, at the same time, imbue with perspective. He’s probably the kindest and most humble brewer I’ve ever had the pleasure of knowing, too. Follow that up with a spectacular team in the kitchen executing food of time and place, and hospitality that is as earnest as it is graceful. And the location can’t be beat. When you go to Fine Creek, you’re anchored in a relationship: with the beer, with the people, and with the very space itself.” —Josh Chapman, CEO and production director, Sojourn Fermentory, Suffolk, Va.

“Hands down, Fox Farm. World-class beer across all styles. One of the prettiest taprooms with exceptional hospitality. They welcome you onto the scenic property like you’re a neighbor.” —Ian Smith, hospitality and operations manager, King’s County Brewer’s Collective, Brooklyn

“The Brewery at Four Star Farms in Northfield, Mass. They brew their beers from grain and hops grown on their very own farm, so everything is so unique and fresh. Chris, the brewer, is amazing and so smart in all aspects of brewing. The owners are wonderful, and the place is just a vacation for the eyes. There’s nothing like true farm-to-glass beer, and they really know their craft.” —Sarah Real, owner and head brewer, Hot Plate Brewing Co., Pittsfield, Mass.

“I think the most underrated is Hot Plate Brewing in Pittsfield, Mass. It’s Latina-owned and just incredible. Every beer Sarah makes is true to style, and she is so intentional with her beer storytelling. She’s doing so much in her community that the beer is just a small part of what makes Hot Plate so special.” —Erica DeAnda, head brewer, Tumbled Rock Brewery and Kitchen, Baraboo, Wis.

“I was recently in OBX (the Outer Banks) and ran across Whalehead Brewery: Love the beer these guys are slinging, especially their award-winning lagers. They’re also utilizing a pour-your-own system. Pretty awesome!” —Liz Hess, owner and brewer, Alley Brews Brewery and Coffee Shop, Denver

“Plan Bee, I know they aren’t the normative New York brewery, but they have been putting out solid craft for years and just chilling upstate. Places like Plan Bee matter. They get us back to the roots and the exciting part of making beer that is quality. They use all N.Y.-sourced ingredients in most of what they produce. Can’t think of anything more legendary.” —Sarah Cervera, brewer, Big Country Organic Brewing, Austin

“The East Coast obviously has some old-school heavy hitters like Victory, Dogfish, and Allagash, and in recent years got the claim to fame of creating a distinctive style of beer with NEIPA, which has given birth to a new wave of famed breweries. But what’s been really exciting to watch in these recent years is how the East Coast has really cultivated a diverse and wonderful craft beer culture that has become truly impressive in such a short span of time. One of my favorite East Coast breweries that doesn’t get as much national recognition is Benchtop Brewing out of Norfolk, Va. Benchtop was doing craft lagers before they were trendy, and they do an amazing job — even foeder-aging most brews — to create a rounded and wonderful flavor that should put Norfolk on any beer drinker’s map.” —Jared Pulliam, head brewer and owner, Lost Generation Brewing, Washington, D.C.

“I love what Eamoni Collier is doing with Urban Garden Brewing in D.C. The whole place feels deeply personal — from her family’s roots in the city’s go-go scene to the vinyl, Black art, and plants from her great-aunt filling the brewery. It’s cool, it’s completely genuine, and more people should be talking about it.” —Zahra Tabatabai, founder, Back Home Beer, New York City

“I would say Hourglass Brewing in Longwood, Fla.is one of the most underrated breweries on the East Coast. They have an incredible team, with longtime staff and a great atmosphere. Their core Double IPA, 2 Million Bees and Some Hops, is one of my favorite beers of all time. Incorporating orange blossom honey into the brew really makes the hops sing. They always have a rotation of fun and funky sours in addition to a plentiful tap list. I go back every time I have the chance to visit!” —Emily Hall, brewer, Other Half Brewery, Brooklyn

“So many breweries deserve to be called out here. I think the most underrated breweries are the ones exclusively brewing with East Coast-grown ingredients. The freshness and distinctive character of those beers really shine through, and I believe it is the future of brewing in the States.” —Jonny Ifergan, co-founder and lead brewer, Niteglow, Brooklyn

content:
This episode of The Buildout is brought to you by Farmer’s Gin. As a bartender, I get to taste a lot of gin, so I can be picky about what I offer my guests. Farmer’s Gin is one of those bottles I keep coming back to, because it delivers exactly what I’m looking for behind the bar. It’s clean, balanced, and makes a fantastic Martini, but it also shines in classics like a Negroni, Gimlet, or even an Alaska. What I really appreciate is how many different drinkers it appeals to. There’s enough juniper for London Dry fans, but also beautiful floral and citrus notes to win over those who prefer softer, more modern gins. It’s one of those bottles guests love because it just tastes great. If you care about quality and well-made cocktails, check out Farmer’s Gin. Follow them at @farmersgin or visit farmersgin.com.

Max Reis was hooked from the first time he visited Mexico. What began as an obsession grew into a deep passion for Mexican spirits, eventually making Reis one of the foremost authorities on the agave-based spirits category in America. That led him to open Mírate and Daisy, two Mexican spirits-focused bars serving some of the most exciting and inventive cocktails in the country — all while honoring the spirits, traditions, and people who make them.

Today on “The Buildout,” Max joins Adam to talk about his journey, how he views the current Los Angeles bar scene, and why honoring the people and culture of Mexico remains central to his work.

title: Ask a Wine Pro: What Is Pink Chardonnay?
summary:
Grown in almost every major winemaking region, there are over 520,000 acres of Chardonnay vines planted around the world. The versatile white grape is notorious for its somewhat divisive nature, with expressions ranging from rich and buttery to fresh and zingy. Though the grape is ubiquitous at wine shops and restaurants, there’s one particular type of Chardonnay that might come as a surprise when you see it on a label or shelf talker: Pink Chardonnay.

content:
Grown in almost every major winemaking region, there are over 520,000 acres of Chardonnay vines planted around the world. The versatile white grape is notorious for its somewhat divisive nature, with expressions ranging from rich and buttery to fresh and zingy. Though the grape is ubiquitous at wine shops and restaurants, there’s one particular type of Chardonnay that might come as a surprise when you see it on a label or shelf talker: Pink Chardonnay.

Not to be confused with rosé wine — made with short macerations of red grapes — Pink Chardonnay (also known as Chardonnay Rose) is a rare, pink-skinned mutation of the classic Chardonnay grape. Though obscure, a few winemakers embraced the oddly pigmented grape, crafting expressions that showcase the variety’s distinct characteristics. Among them is natural wine luminary Stéphane Tissot. Based in France’s Jura region, Tissot is credited with being among the first to bottle Chardonnay Rose as a single varietal wine.

Elsewhere, the grape is catching on: Last year, Champagne included the grape on its list of permissible varieties. Still, there are just a handful of winemakers around the world who work with Pink Chardonnay and even fewer who produce single varietal expressions.

Like other grapes whose popularity resulted from propagation — such as Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc — Pink Chardonnay’s future is reliant on the curious winemakers who decide to clip and replant the mutation. When Tissot first spotted the pink berries, he used massal selection to expand the vine.

“I bought an old vineyard in 2004, and in the middle of it there were around 30 bunches of Chardonnay Rose,” says Tissot, who farms in Arbois. “And from that, I picked and selected a handful and planted almost one hectare in total.”

Most Pink Chardonnay savants say the grape first popped up in Burgundy in the early 1900s. The mutation is similar to the mother grape in most respects other than its slightly lower acidity and rosy skin. And, as Tissot puts it: “It’s just a little bit more rustic, a bit less fragile, a bit firmer, a bit more dense than typical Chardonnay.”

Though the grape long remained relatively close to its place of origin, there is now an example coming from the San Luis Obispo Coast. Rajat Parr, whose collective of wineries includes Phelan Farm, Scythian Wine Co., and Brij Wines, works with cool-climate varieties on California’s Central Coast. For the Phelan Farm label, he focuses on grapes from the Jura and adjacent alpine regions, such as Poulsard, Trousseau, Mondeuse. He also farms a special parcel of Pink Chardonnay — the first produced in the U.S.

“It grows very much like regular Chardonnay,” Parr says. “You have to pick it when the skins are ripe and when they are pink. So, it needs to grow in a cool climate because if it’s grown in a warm place, then it’ll lose all of its acidity by time it gets that color.”

Much of the sudden spark of interest in the pink-berried Chardonnay mutation can be credited to Jura’s recent rise in popularity, largely propelled by beloved niche producers like Tissot. Because of the number of old vine Chardonnay plots in Jura, the region has become something of a breeding ground for mutations and experimental wines, Tissot says.

Pink Chardonnay has become a hobby horse among certain winos, particularly the natural wine set. With such a small number of plantings, the production of Chardonnay Rose remains very limited. Tissot estimates he yields only 2,000 to 4,000 bottles of his Chardonnay Rose cuvée ‘Rose Massale’ a year. Parr estimates only 20 to 50 cases each vintage — and sells nearly all of it on a direct-to-consumer mailing list.

Tira Johnson, corporate beverage director for the We All Gotta Eat Group offers single varietal expressions of Pink Chardonnay on her heavy-hitting bottle lists at New York City restaurants Chez Fifi and Sushi Noz. While there’s the occasional pedantic, “Chardonnay-can’t-make-a-rosé” diner, Johnson enjoys the opportunity to present a familiar but altogether new grape to her clients.

“It’s an especially fun adventure for Burgundy and Jura drinkers,” Johnson, who went down a self-described Pink Chardonnay rabbit hole, says. “I love introducing them to something new and different that’s not so wild and crazy. Pink Chardonnays have a really beautiful texture. I don’t notice a huge difference from regular Chardonnay, but there is something so special about it.”

While many, if not most, wine drinkers are unaware of the grape, its inclusion as a permissible variety in Champagne brought Pink Chardonnay some level of worldwide recognition last year. While producers in the region have yet to fully welcome the new addition, Tissot and Johnson both believe many Champagne producers will begin to plant the mutation.

“I don’t know of any Champagne producers that are doing singular Chardonnay Rose bottlings, but I could totally see producers like Laherte Frères doing that — people who love experimenting with different grape varieties,” Johnson says. “I think it’s such a cool, compelling wine, and 20 years from now, it could be a relevant grape variety.”

title: The 20 Best Merlots for 2026
summary:
Merlot is thought to be named after Merle (or Merlau), a local bird in the Bordeaux region of France. Whether this is true or not, it can be helpful to think of Merlot as the little blackbird of Bordeaux. It’s the softening ingredient to Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc: it has more flesh between the skin and fewer seeds than many other grapes, which can result in supple, deep, and fleshy red wine. And though it’s primarily known for its role in blends, Merlot can certainly shine on its own.

content:
Merlot is thought to be named after Merle (or Merlau), a local bird in the Bordeaux region of France. Whether this is true or not, it can be helpful to think of Merlot as the little blackbird of Bordeaux. It’s the softening ingredient to Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc: it has more flesh between the skin and fewer seeds than many other grapes, which can result in supple, deep, and fleshy red wine. And though it’s primarily known for its role in blends, Merlot can certainly shine on its own.

Despite some notable setbacks for the grape in the U.S., winemakers across the country are still making thoughtful expressions of Merlot. We tasted a wide swath of expressions from New York and Virginia to California and Oregon (plus a bright expression from Italy) and came away with the same take we’ve had all along: Merlot rocks.

Here are the 20 best Merlots to drink in 2026.

Table of Contents

  • Best Merlots Under $25

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Why You Should Trust VinePair
Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.
Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year. This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.
VinePair’s tasting panel evaluates every wine on its aromas, flavors, structure, balance, and quality. We also consider whether or not the wine showed typicity for its specific grape or region.

How We Compiled This List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Merlots to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

For the Merlot roundup, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of best Merlots to buy right now. Each wine was assessed on quality, price, and availability to compile the final list.

The Best Value Merlot

Frei Brothers Merlot 2024

Affordable red wine is everywhere on our market. We try a lot of it here at VinePair, so when one absolutely floors us, it’s a big deal. This Merlot is one of them.

Sourced from two estate vineyards in Sonoma’s Dry Creek Valley, this wine opens with soft, ripe fruit notes of blackberries, black cherry, and plum. There’s a layer of rich vanilla and spice from aging in French and American oak for nine months, adding a warming depth. The mouthfeel is plush and deep with great acidity. This is a case buy and an excellent house red.

Average price: $20
Rating: 92

See Review

The Best Splurge Merlot

Wölffer Estate Vineyard Christian’s Cuvée Merlot 2020

Winemakers in the U.S. have long taken a cue from France’s Bordeaux region, gravitating toward grape varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. This is particularly true in Long Island, a waterfront winegrowing area that first built its reputation on Bordeaux-style blends. But this Merlot-focused bottling brings an entirely new, unique expression of the variety. Where the West Coast coaxes out the depth and sun in its wines, Long Island’s crisp ocean breezes help the variety express its more elegant side. One is not better than the other, and that’s the beauty of American wine: we just have multiple styles on offer at any given time.

Roman Roth, winemaker at Wölffer, understands this and produces an absolutely beautiful Merlot. Blueberries, campfire smoke, and a distant hint of brewed coffee emerge on the nose. The mouthfeel is pure elegance, with delicate touches of sandalwood and cinnamon accenting the ripe fruit. It has an almost-perfect medium fruit depth and acidity that lifts each element off the palate. A gorgeous wine.

The Best of the Rest:

Best Merlots Under $25

Wente Family Vineyards Sandstone Merlot 2023

The Wente family has successfully produced one of the best affordable Merlots on the market. Sourced from hillside vineyards on California’s Central Coast, influenced by ocean breezes, this bottle brings lively notes of black and blue fruits with a dusting of mocha on the nose. The palate is soft, plush, and fleshy with a very well-balanced fruit core. Get this now.

The wine brings notes of blueberries, soil, and a hint of savory nori, with some added depth from 12 months of aging in both French and American oak. Friulian Merlot is an underestimated gem. Italy’s hilly Friuli region is primarily known for its white wines, but it also produces some stunning — and remarkably fresh — expressions of a few distinct red grapes, including Merlot. This bottling from Paraschos is pure earthy fruitiness, with aromas of tart cherries, strawberries, balsamic, smoke, and spice wafting about. FAQs

What kind of wine is Merlot?

Merlot is a red grape variety known for being soft, ripe, elegant, and easy to drink. It originated in the Bordeaux region of France and is the second most popular red grape in America after Cabernet Sauvignon.

Is Merlot a good wine for beginners?

Merlot is often recommended as one of the first varieties someone new to red wine should drink due to its approachability, plummy taste, and soft characteristics.

Is Merlot a strong wine?

Merlot wines typically contain around 13.5 percent ABV but can approach 14.5 percent and beyond, especially when grown in the warmer climates of Australia, California, or Chile.

The article The 10 Most Expensive Tequilas in the World (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Though many consumers might recognize tequila as what they encountered in a shot in college or as the ingredient in their favorite cocktail, there’s also a market for extremely high-end tequila.

These luxury bottles, often from prestigious brands like Clase Azul and Patrón, are revered for both their flavor profiles and elaborate presentations — many are sold in artisanal decanters made in collaboration with esteemed artists. But beyond the substance of what’s in the bottle and style of the packaging, exclusivity is also a factor in the premium tequila market: The most coveted bottlings often come from limited-production runs of under 500 bottles in total.

From anniversary releases to extra añejos, here are the most expensive tequilas in the world, according to Wine Searcher.

10. Clase Azul Eduardo Sarabia Limited Edition Tequila Joven, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul collaborated with Mexican-American contemporary artist Eduard Sarabia for this limited-edition release. This Joven blend — of which only 450 exist — combines Clase Azul blanco, Russian oak-aged añejo, and sherry cask-aged añejo.

  • Average price: $8,691
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Citrus, vanilla, caramel

9. Patrón Limited Edition En Lalique Serie 2 Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

The second edition of Patrón’s En Lalique series — released in 2017 — was aged for eight years in American oak, French oak, and ex-sherry barrels with just 299 bottles hitting markets.

  • Average price: $8,839
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Honey, citrus fruit, oak

8. Clase Azul Puebla Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

This extra-aged tequila from Clase Azul, which matures in antique French barrels, is produced as an homage to the Battle of Puebla. There are only 300 hand-numbered bottles in existence.

  • Average price: $9,358
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Baking spice, dried fruit, toasted oak

7. Dos Armadillos ‘Sterling Silver’ Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

This luxe bottling from Dos Armadillos is a twice-distilled tequila aged for over eight years. The ornate clay decanter is decorated with sterling silver.

  • Average price: $10,000
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Fruit jam, vanilla, oak

6. Patrón Limited Edition En Lalique Serie 3 Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

Patrón’s third series of its En Lalique lineup released in 2022 and is an extra añejo housed in crystal decanters.

  • Average price: $10,947
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Honey, dried fruit, oak

5. Clase Azul Master Artisans Canela Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul’s Canela from the Master Artisans series is an extra añejo finished in ex-American whiskey, ex-amontillado sherry, and ex-Madeira casks.

  • Average price: $15,001
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Cooked agave, dark chocolate, caramel

4. Clase Azul ‘Jalisco 200’ Limited Edition Tequila Extra Añejo, Jalisco, Mexico

Clase Azul crafted the aptly named Jalisco 200 to commemorate the bicentennial of Jalisco as a Mexican state.

  • Average price: $12,651
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Molasses, honey, roasted agave

3. Clase Azul Master Artisans Guirnalda Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Guirnalda from Clase Azul’s Master Artisans lineup was aged for over eight years, moving from American whiskey casks to sherry barrels to finishing in Madeira casks.

  • Average price: $13,200
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Fig, almond, oak

2. Clase Azul Master Artisans Cobalto Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Another expression from Clase Azul’s Master Artisans collection, the Cobalto was created in collaboration with master artisan Jesús Guerrero Santos.

  • Average price: $15,001
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Dried fruit, citrus, honey

1. Clase Azul Master Artisans Angel Santos Limited Edition Tequila, Jalisco, Mexico

Rounding out the Master Artisans — and all Clase Azuls on this list — is the limited-edition Angel Santos. Only 300 bottles of this highly coveted extra añejo were released to markets.

  • Average price: $17,700
  • ABV: 40%
  • Tasting notes: Agave, autumnal spice, dried fruit

title: We Asked 11 Bartenders: What’s the Best Rye for Beginners? (2026)
summary:
Unlike the approachably sweet vanilla and caramel flavors of corn-based bourbon, rye whiskey’s unique base delivers a distinct spice note that might turn off some first-timers. But once immersed in the category, rye’s savory qualities make it an essential tool in an at-home bartending arsenal, ideal for adding an extra kick to any whiskey cocktail. Though bourbon may be the go-to gateway whiskey, bartenders celebrate — and sometimes prefer — rye for its more robust, complex taste.

The article We Asked 11 Bartenders: What’s the Best Rye for Beginners? (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Unlike the approachably sweet vanilla and caramel flavors of corn-based bourbon, rye whiskey’s unique base delivers a distinct spice note that might turn off some first-timers. But once immersed in the category, rye’s savory qualities make it an essential tool in an at-home bartending arsenal, ideal for adding an extra kick to any whiskey cocktail.

Though bourbon may be the go-to gateway whiskey, bartenders celebrate — and sometimes prefer — rye for its more robust, complex taste. Those behind the stick are most attuned to the variety of rye whiskeys available and know the specific bottles that are most welcoming to newcomers’ palates. That’s why we asked 11 bartenders to name the rye whiskey they think is the best bet for a newbie. From well-known brands to small-batch distilleries, here’s what they had to say.

The best rye for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Michter’s US*1 Rye
  • Elijah Craig Rye
  • Rittenhouse Rye Bottled-in-Bond
  • Bulleit Rye
  • Knob Creek 7 Year Old Rye
  • Fort Hamilton Single Barrel Rye Whiskey
  • Woodford Reserve Rye
  • Sazerac Rye

“My recommendation for a beginner rye whiskey would be Michter’s US*1 Rye. Many people approach rye expecting an intensely spicy or pepper-forward whiskey, but Michter’s offers a much softer introduction to the category. It delivers classic rye character while maintaining a rounded profile of caramel, vanilla, orange peel, baking spice, and light oak. What makes it particularly approachable is its balance: It has enough rye spice to demonstrate what sets the category apart from bourbon, but not so much that it becomes polarizing for newer whiskey drinkers. Whether enjoyed neat, on a large cube, or in a Manhattan or Old Fashioned, it provides an excellent foundation for understanding rye whiskey.” —Zack Flack, head bartender, The National, Autograph Collection, Oklahoma City

“Elijah Craig Rye is a fantastic place to start for beginners entering the rye world. To me, rye whiskey is like the cooler cousin to bourbon: It’s more sophisticated, nuanced, and flavorful compared to most entry-level bourbons. Elijah Craig Rye is not only marked at an affordable price, making it easy for your wallet, but also at a higher-than-average proof, which shines in cocktails or just over some ice.” —Zachariah Brown, head bartender, Point Seven, New York City

“I believe Rittenhouse Rye is the perfect starter rye. I naturally reach for higher-proof spirits when building cocktails, and at 100 proof, this one always fits the bill without getting lost. Its affordability and accessibility make it an easy choice, while the notes of dried fruit and lingering warm spice hit every fall craving. Sitting at exactly 51 percent rye, it’s the perfect ‘bridge’ whiskey for future enthusiasts.” —Stephanie Cohen, head bartender, The Port of Call, Mystic, Conn.

“Bulleit Rye is my choice for introducing beginners to rye whiskey, as its versatility works beautifully across applications. The flavor profile is compelling and accessible, presenting a clear range of flavors that are easy to understand while reflecting the classic characteristics found in traditional rye whiskey. At Millie Leigh’s, we’re aging Bulleit Rye in four-gallon casks for a few months to provide something different to our guests with the possibility of enjoying this rye in our version of an Old Fashioned made with vanilla syrup.” —Hugo Duffaut, beverage manager, Millie Leigh’s, Midland, Texas

“If I’m reaching for what I’d consider a beginner friendly rye, I’m assuming it’s for a bourbon drinker who’s ready to make the jump. Knob Creek 7 Year Old Rye ticks all the boxes for me. It has a high-corn mash bill which helps temper some of that rye spice and makes for an easier transition for most bourbon drinkers. It’s bottled at 100 proof with a seven year age statement, so there’s no shortage of complexity, texture, or weight on the palate without being too hot. And as far as value, Knob Creek has been punching above its weight in terms of quality versus price. Start with Knob Creek, and if you like what you see and are ready to graduate, cross the river to Indiana and check out some of the MGP bottlings next.” —Beck Hargrave, bartender, Oiji Mi, NYC

“Bulleit Rye is the best rye whiskey for beginners because of its approachable yet classic flavor profile. Known for its high-rye content — 95 percent rye and 5 percent malted barley — it offers a crisp, spicy character that defines the category. Despite the spice, it remains incredibly smooth, featuring gentle notes of vanilla, honey, and oak. This balance makes it smooth enough to sip neat, yet robust enough to stand out in classic cocktails like a Manhattan or an Old Fashioned. Affordable and widely available, it is the perfect introduction to rye!” —Valentin Bouteiller, bartender, Local 101 Beaurepaire, Paris

“Fort Hamilton Single Barrel Rye is a perfect choice for the beginner rye drinker. Distilled in Brooklyn, N.Y., from a mash bill of 90 percent rye and 10 percent malted barley and aged for minimum of five years, this 45 percent ABV rye is very approachable — it’s spicy but balanced with enough alcohol to show ‘character’ but without cask-strength intensity. You can detect caramel, cinnamon, mint, white pepper, oak, and lemon. It’s exceptionally rich with lots of texture and perfect for cocktails or to sip neat.” —Amir Babayoff, beverage director, Ophelia Lounge, NYC

“I would tell folks to start with the brand of bourbon they like and see if the same distillery also produces rye. I really enjoy Knob Creek Rye as an intro — it’s sweet but runs a tad hot with complexity emerging as you drink. Other ones would be Woodford Reserve Rye and Sazerac Rye. A good price range to stick to is $35 to $75 a bottle. Some may say it’s pedestrian, but I say drink what you like.” —Danielle Goldtooth, founder, Dii IINÀ, Phoenix

“Rittenhouse is great for beginners because it mixes so well. It’s a little higher proof, but that just means more rye flavor comes through. Cut it with a bit of cognac in a Sazerac, and you won’t be disappointed.” —Ian Alexander, beverage director, Limo Bar, NYC

“For beginners, I think Michter’s Rye is a great place to start. The mash bill is relatively low in rye, so while you still get that characteristic spice that you expect, it still feels a little more approachable for people who might be more accustomed to drinking bourbon. It holds up in classic rye-based cocktails but can also be enjoyed on its own without being overwhelming.” —Kat Foster, beverage director, Marlow East, NYC

“Rittenhouse Rye Bottled-in-Bond is a great starter rye because it’s approachable, affordable, and still gives you that classic spicy rye character. At 100 proof, it has enough backbone to stand up to vermouth, bitters, citrus, and other bold cocktail ingredients without getting lost, making it an absolute workhorse behind the bar.” —Libby Lingua, owner and bartender, Highball, Phoenix

title: The Bull Case for Sierra Nevada’s Under-the-Radar ‘Hype Brewery’ Line
summary:
A problem — the problem? — for first-generation craft breweries is as follows. 1. Everybody knows your iconic beer. 2. Everybody loves your iconic beer. 3. Nobody buys your iconic beer. We have contemplated this paradox many times here at Hop Take over the years. Recall the disastrous redesign Sapporo USA Sapporo Stone Brewing Sapporo USA put poor Anchor Brewing Company through at the beginning of this decade. Lament the ignominious demise of the original source of Leinenkugel’s beloved shandy. Bear witness to the regrettable unraveling of Rogue Ales & Spirits. And so on and so forth.

The article The Bull Case for Sierra Nevada’s Under-the-Radar ‘Hype Brewery’ Line appeared first on VinePair.
content:
A problem — the problem? — for first-generation craft breweries is as follows.

1. Everybody knows your iconic beer.
2. Everybody loves your iconic beer.
3. Nobody buys your iconic beer.

We have contemplated this paradox many times here at Hop Take over the years. Recall the disastrous redesign Sapporo USA Sapporo Stone Brewing Sapporo USA put poor Anchor Brewing Company through at the beginning of this decade. Lament the ignominious demise of the original source of Leinenkugel’s beloved shandy. Bear witness to the regrettable unraveling of Rogue Ales & Spirits. And so on and so forth.

Complicating matters, pioneering breweries face a double-bind as they try to breathe new life into old brands. I framed up the problem in January 2023 about New Belgium Brewery’s then-new facelift for Fat Tire:

If Fat Tire were an actual bicycle, most people would put it on Craigslist and call it a day. But New Belgium can’t toss its former glory on the junk heap just yet. Even as younger drinkers gravitate toward the Voodoo Ranger clan’s bolder flavors and packaging, there are plenty of Gen Xers and Millennials with plenty of money for whom Fat Tire represents the golden era of early 21st-century American craft brewing. People still drink it! And despite its diminished stature, Fat Tire is still a top-20 craft brand overall. So New Belgium went for an overhaul instead, reformulating a “crisper, brighter” liquid and giving it a slick new package that calls attention to its eco-friendly credentials and omits its middling 5 percent ABV and outmoded style. “There’s a challenge to recharge heritage brands,” New Belgium vice president of marketing Kyle Bradshaw told Brewbound earlier this month, adding that the move “feels like a big risk” given Fat Tire’s outsized legacy.

That’s the rub. The American drinking public likes the idea of these classic craft beers much more than it actually likes buying them. To tinker with them too much is to invite much nostalgic gnashing of teeth; to leave them entirely untinkered with, to embrace decline.

Next year, Sierra Nevada Brewing Company — purveyor of the eponymous, irreproachable Pale Ale since 1980 — will take its biggest steps yet down the middle path. It’s been a long time coming.

“Five or six years ago when I started with Sierra, you know, one of the things that we were having to overcome was this perception of being ‘grocery store craft,’” says Kyle Ingram, Sierra Nevada’s senior director of innovation, in a phone interview with Hop Take. “Which is not quite an endearing term, not one that we were super proud of.”

The California outfit, which just last year edged out fellow first-waver Boston Beer Company in Brewers Association-defined craft beer barrelage, worked the problem from multiple angles. It recently unveiled its plans to refresh the packaging on a slate of core portfolio brands, including — gasp — Pale Ale itself in fall 2027. “Our portfolio had developed over such a long period of time that it didn’t look coherent on display, and I think some of it had aged and we needed to shake the dust off,” Sierra Nevada chief executive Pryce Greenow explained to Brewbound at a wholesaler conference at its North Carolina plant last month.

It bears mentioning that the company is actually embarking on that tightrope walk from a position of relative strength. According to multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, Sierra Nevada’s portfolio grew 1.9 percent in dollars and 0.2 percent in case volume year-to-date through September 6, outpacing the declining category and the even-more-rapidly declining craft segment within it.

Perhaps emboldened by that trend-bucking performance, the invigoration effort won’t stop with refreshes, though. “When you have a healthy core, it allows you to innovate in a way where we’re not dependent on that [new] thing being big and successful right out of the gate,” says Ingram.

To that end, Sierra Nevada has cued up two of its boldest portfolio expansions in recent memory. Crafted By Sierra Nevada, a line featuring “spiked agave seltzer” (read: hard seltzer) Agua Azul and “beer soda” (read: radler) Shred, marks the firm’s first major foray into the “beyond beer” space since it spun up and wound down also-ran entrants Tea West and Strainge Beast earlier this decade. The new fermentables are already on (or soon to hit) shelves in test markets bearing subordinated branding from the mothership.

“The question has always been can we win in those spaces without leveraging the awareness and the credibility of the Sierra Nevada brand, but also to do so without disparaging or diluting the equity of the Sierra Nevada brand for a loyal beer drinker?” says Ingram, to whom fell the unenviable responsibility of pitching founder Ken Grossman on a beer soda called Shred. “I remember thinking distinctly, this might be my last pitch,” he tells Hop Take, laughing.

Whether Craft By Sierra Nevada’s offerings can thrive — or even survive — in a lucrative-but-tricky flavored malt beverage pseudosegment dominated by scaled flavor-chasers like Mark Anthony Group, Anheuser-Busch InBev, and BBC remains to be seen. But to your humble Hop Take columnist’s eye, the thesis on those products is sound.

This brings us to the Hidden Scroll series. Unlike Crafted By, this new “brand family” is composed of honest-to-goodness beers, but it is tasked with a more ambitious goal. Namely: to score big, consistent Sierra Nevada some of the lucre and latter-day cachet of small, dynamic “hype breweries.”

“That guy who is paying 25 bucks for a four-pack, he’s looking for some of the more local, the more ‘hype’ kind of breweries in that space,” says Ingram. “We’re certainly capable and credible from a brewing standpoint, but maybe that’s not the area of the shelf or the cooler where people are looking for Sierra Nevada.” Building on the promise of West Ghost India Pale Ale — a semi-branded offering that made the transition from taproom-only bestseller to national packaged distribution in early 2026 — the company has formalized its higher-pricepoint ambitions under Hidden Scroll, so named because beers under this aegis will not feature the venerable gold sheafing that adorns labels in the core portfolio.

“That’s the first thing we want people to see, it’s the thing that brings that credibility, but we weren’t sure that it was working to our advantage in this space,” says Ingram of the scroll design. Instead: “Let’s grab shoppers’ attention with really cool modern artwork, because that’s a lot of how these guys shop.” He should know — by his own admission, he’s one of them.

For 2027, Sierra Nevada has retooled West Ghost’s packaging, and is deliberating over which of the other Hidden Scrolls beers it’s been testing in its taprooms it will put into 4-packs and push into distribution. Potential options include Boat Plane, a West Coast Pilsner, and Lava Lamp, a double IPA. The cans feature art-forward designs printed on the white matte labeling that’s become a visual lingua franca among more specialty craft offerings. There’s very little obvious connection to the brewery from whence they came but for a “Sierra Nevada Brewing Co., Chico, CA & Mills River, NC” demarcation along the bottom in small letters, and a faint scroll that’s been blended — hidden — into the illustration.

“People aren’t grabbing it because it’s from Sierra Nevada, they’re finding out that it’s from Sierra Nevada after they’ve already thrown a couple back,” says Ingram. “It’s been wildly successful for us, relative to the size of the category. We had a hard time keeping up with the volume in the first few months.”

Here, another rub. A core appeal of “hype” beers — to the extent that such appeal still exists at scale as we enter the back half of the ‘20s — is their scarcity, esotericism, and rapid-fire release cadence. Would, say, Other Half Brewing Company’s offerings have captivated finance bros late last decade if they were available in a dozen states, rather than only via a hole-in-the-wall across the street from a McDonald’s in central Brooklyn? Or, asked another way, is that sort of “hype” compatible with a Sierra Nevada sort of craft brewery?

I ask Ingram to square this circle.

For all Sierra Nevada’s logistical and technical advantages, “we have some disadvantages too. We’re not built to do small things really, really fast,” he concedes. “We’re not really designed to. That’s not the game that we’re playing, but we still feel like we can have a meaningful place in this category.”

Can Hidden Scroll find a place among the hype beer pantheon? Can Crafted By Sierra Nevada succeed where previous beyond-beer bids have failed? Can this four-decade firm bust the double-bind that has hemmed in so many craft beer brands of a certain age? Sierra Nevada has put together a compelling case. But only John Q. Guzzler can make the call.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

It’s no secret that Boston Beer Company has struggled mightily marketing-wise over the past few years. So the fact that it has a new chief marketing officer lined up isn’t surprising. But Allison Stransky, who starts October 12, has a resume that ought to raise some eyebrows: she’s taking this job after serving as the marketing lead for Samsung Electronics America. Can you pitch Samuel Adams the same way you pitch smartphones? Trade wisdom holds that you cannot. But we’ll see!
